strengths: MaskSub provides a useful, technically coherent way to incorporate strong masking into supervised training. The shared-weight, asymmetric distillation objective is simple to implement and introduces no inference overhead.

The central empirical contribution is well supported. Table 1 reports improvements of 0.3–0.7 percentage points across four ViT sizes and two training lengths using strong DeiT-III baselines. Positive results also extend to ResNet, Swin, and several pretrained-model fine-tuning recipes.

Comparisons at similar training cost substantiate practical value beyond simply adding computation. In Table 7, ViT-B reaches 84.1% in 25 GPU-days versus 83.7% in 26 GPU-days for longer baseline training. Table 8 also shows better accuracy than CoSub with lower training cost.

The appendix provides meaningful evidence beyond ImageNet classification: improvements on ADE20K, COCO, and multiple distribution-shift benchmarks. For example, ViT-B ImageNet-A accuracy increases from 36.8% to 41.9% in Table A.4. These results strengthen the contribution to visual representation learning.

Reproducibility is supported by concise pseudocode, detailed training configurations, masking-ratio and loss-weight ablations, and three-run statistics for selected experiments. Together, the breadth and controlled comparisons provide a stronger case for acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is moderate: the contribution combines established masking, shared-weight self-distillation, and asymmetric supervision. Comparisons with CoSub and GradAug are useful, but Table 6 compares self-distillation methods under different training recipes. Those results cannot establish the claimed incompatibility of earlier methods with stronger recipes.

The explanation of automatic difficulty control exceeds the evidence. In Eq. (3), the masked-logit gradient depends on the difference between masked and main-model probabilities, rather than whether the main prediction is correct. A confidently incorrect teacher can therefore provide substantial erroneous supervision. Figure 3 supports changing auxiliary-gradient strength, but does not establish that masking supervision is restricted to successfully learned examples.

The distillation ablation needs clearer specification. Table A.6 describes removing KD loss without stating whether the masked branch instead receives ground-truth supervision or loses its training objective entirely. Consequently, the manuscript does not clearly isolate soft-target supervision from the benefit of retaining a clean supervised branch.

The broad improvement claims require qualification. With MaskSub-pretrained ViT-B, adding MaskSub during fine-tuning reduces CIFAR-100 accuracy from 91.9% to 89.6% in Table 10. Section 4.2 also states that the best CLIP fine-tuning accuracy matches the baseline. Several transfer improvements are small relative to reported variability, while BEiTv2's 0.1-point gains lack uncertainty estimates. These limitations temper universal applicability, although they do not overturn the stronger central results.

Efficiency and reporting claims need tighter wording. Figure 2 demonstrates convergence improvement per epoch, without establishing faster wall-clock convergence; training overhead remains approximately 45% for the tested ViT and doubles for hierarchical architectures. Separately, two readily correctable numerical errors are present: Table 9's 8.6 versus 23.4 GPU-days does not support the stated one-sixth total cost, and Table 10's ViT-S Cars improvement is 11.3 points rather than 1.3.
